messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Akua had always found solace in the natural world. As a park ranger, she spent her days surrounded by the sights and sounds of wildlife, and her evenings exploring the trails with her husband, Kwame. But everything changed when Kwame was killed in a sudden accident on one of those trails. The memory of that day is etched in Akua's mind like a photograph - every detail, from the sunlight filtering through the trees to the sound of her own screams. In the months since Kwame's death, Akua has struggled to come to terms with her new reality. She had always defined herself by her role as a wife and partner, and now that was gone. "I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me," she says, her voice barely above a whisper. This feeling of loss has seeped into every aspect of her life, leaving her feeling emotionally numb, like she's just going through the motions. Akua believes that she has permanently changed for the worse, and this negative self-appraisal has led her to drop important responsibilities at work, afraid that she'll fail or make a mistake. As Akua navigates her daily routine, she finds herself constantly on alert, her body tense and ready to react to danger. She has trouble sleeping, haunted by vivid dreams and fragmented memories of the accident. When these sudden pieces of memory appear, they bring with them overwhelming grief, and Akua is transported back to that terrible day. These intrusions have become so distressing that Akua has begun to avoid relaxing or engaging in activities she used to enjoy, fearing that they'll trigger another painful memory. Akua's maladaptive strategies are an attempt to cope with these memories and the emotions they evoke. She keeps her mind occupied all the time, whether it's by working long hours or engaging in mentally demanding tasks. By avoiding relaxation, Akua feels like she can stay one step ahead of her memories, but this only serves to reinforce the cycle. The more she avoids, the more memories seem to intrude, and the more convinced she becomes that she is no longer capable of living a normal life. As the weeks have turned into months, Akua's avoidance behaviors have started to take a toll on her relationships with colleagues and friends. They've noticed a change in her, a distance or preoccupation that they can't quite explain. But for Akua, it feels like she's just trying to survive, one day at a time. She's come to believe that if she can just keep moving, keep working, she might be able to outrun the memories and the grief that threatens to consume her. It was only when Akua found herself unable to perform even routine tasks without feeling overwhelmed by anxiety that she realized she needed help. The thought of facing another day like this is what finally brought her to therapy, hoping to break the cycle of avoidance and learn to live with the memories that haunt her. As she sits in the therapist's office, Akua's body tense and ready to react, she whispers a single phrase: "I just want to be able to feel again."
